Alternatively, merging would require a complex multipart structure including the stream as a part, needing buffering, or a streaming multipart encoder, which would be a significant architectural change.
The error message is "Streamed bodies and files are mutually exclusive", and the `NotImplementedError` signals an unsupported combination by design, not a feature planned for later.

The validation of readonly_fields entries happens in the `_check_readonly_fields_item` method in `django/contrib/admin/checks.py`.
The primary mechanism is a callability check: the method first tests whether `field_name` is callable using Python's built-in `callable()`.
If `field_name` is callable, `_check_readonly_fields_item` immediately returns an empty list, meaning no validation errors; this lets decorated methods pass.
If the item is not callable, the check falls back to attribute existence: `hasattr(obj, field_name)` on the ModelAdmin instance, or `hasattr(obj.model, field_name)` on the model.
As a last resort, it tries `obj.model._meta.get_field(field_name)`, and returns a validation error if this fails.

It decouples symbolic representation from numerical solver implementations through a standardized abstract property interface that defines the structure of the differential equations without specifying their concrete form.
Abstract property `M` returns a square matrix of left-hand side coefficients of the linear ODE system M(x, r, t, p) x' = F(x, r, t, p).
Abstract property `F` returns a column matrix of the right-hand side equations of the same ODE system.

Abstract properties `state_vars` (x), `input_vars` (r) and `constants` (p) return column matrices of the state variables (functions of time), input variables, and non-time-varying symbolic constants respectively.
Abstract property `order` returns the order of the differential equation, and abstract method `rhs()` returns the solution to the ODE system.
Concrete subclasses such as `ZerothOrderActivation` and `FirstOrderActivationDeGroote2016` supply different symbolic expressions but conform to the same interface structure.

Example: `ZerothOrderActivation` (no differential equation) returns an empty `Matrix([])` for `M`, whereas `FirstOrderActivationDeGroote2016` returns `Matrix([Integer(1)])` for `M` and a complex hyperbolic-tangent expression for `F`.

Solvers can work with any subclass by accessing the properties, without needing to know the specific mathematical form, the order of the equation, the state variable structure, or implementation details.
The standardized structure, especially the `constants` property, facilitates automatic code generation for numerical solvers.
The design allows extensibility (new activation models by subclassing) and integration with components like `MusculotendonBase` that accept any `ActivationBase` subclass.
The design follows the Strategy pattern: the abstract base class defines the strategy interface and concrete activation models are interchangeable strategies.

In ASTDeclaratorParen.get_type_id, the declarator following the parentheses (`next`) is processed first, using the original returnTypeId, to produce next_id.

The order reflects C++ declarator syntax of the form `ReturnType (inner)next`, where parentheses change precedence/binding of type modifiers.
The code comment says "ReturnType (inner)next, so 'inner' returns everything outside": inner needs to know what comes after the parentheses to represent the return type structure.
The next part (e.g. pointer operators or array/function suffixes after the parentheses) must be evaluated first so the full type structure outside the parentheses is known.

The current RevisionList has no thread safety: it keeps a plain `_data` list with no locking, so concurrent threads can corrupt it.

ServerStore's `_update_last_revision` does a read-modify-write where the lock is released between the read and the write, so concurrent updates can be lost (e.g. thread B overwrites thread A's rev3 with rev4).
The existing fasteners.InterProcessLock file locking works only on a single machine, so it does not protect distributed server instances, and NFS file locking is unreliable and slow.
The current design has no version tracking, so it cannot detect concurrent modifications or resolve conflicts.
Tier 1 fix: add an internal reentrant lock (threading.RLock) to RevisionList and wrap all operations (loads, dumps, add_revision, latest_revision, get_time, as_list, remove_revision, __eq__) with it.

Tier 1 fix: add an `atomic_update_file(path, update_func, lock_file)` method to the storage adapter (ServerDiskAdapter) that reads, modifies and writes the file inside one lock hold. It writes to a temp file and uses os.replace for an atomic rename. ServerStore's `_update_last_revision` and revision-removal then use it.

Tier 2: add optimistic locking with a VersionedRevisionList that stores a version counter, incremented on every change and persisted in the JSON. `add_revision` returns whether anything changed, and the update is skipped when nothing changed.
Tier 2: retry failed updates with exponential backoff and jitter, up to a maximum number of retries.

Tier 3 Option A: for multiple servers, use a Redis-based distributed lock acquired with SET NX and an expiry, using a unique token per holder. It is released by an atomic check-and-delete Lua script so only the owner releases it. The read-modify-write and the temp-file-plus-rename write happen while the lock is held.

Tier 3 Option B: an eventually consistent CRDT revision list, with last-write-wins entries carrying timestamp, server id and Lamport clock, and a merge operation to sync between servers. It resolves conflicts by timestamp, then clock, then server id as tie-breaker.

Tier 4 (recommended): a hybrid store that uses local file locking with optimistic versioning and retry by default, and Redis distributed locking when a Redis client is configured. It falls back to file-based locking if Redis is unavailable.

The rollout should be backward compatible: loads accepts the old format without a version field and dumps always writes the new format with a version. It is phased (foundation, reliability, distribution, production) with a gradual feature-flag rollout.

Validation relies on concurrency unit tests (many threads adding revisions with no duplicates or corruption), multi-server integration tests, performance benchmarks, and metrics such as lock wait time, conflicts, retries and error rate.

Raising InvalidPropValueError during prop validation incurs performance costs that scale with nesting depth in deeply nested component hierarchies, since each level adds both validation overhead and exception handling costs.
String formatting overhead: each error constructs a detailed message containing component names and prop lists using string joins and formatting operations.
Exception propagation: in nested hierarchies the exception must unwind through multiple component initialization layers.
Python's exception handling destroys intermediate states at each level of unwinding.
Validation cascade: when nested components fail validation, parent components may need to handle cleanup or re-validation, creating multiplicative costs across hierarchy depth.
Memory pressure: exception objects capture stack traces and keep component references during unwinding.
Those retained references prevent immediate garbage collection of failed component subtrees.

Using a single shared instance (singleton) instead of creating new instances each time significantly reduces memory overhead when there are many parameter checks.
`_Unset` is a sentinel class defined in `lib/matplotlib/_api/__init__.py` (lines 32-35), with a `__repr__` returning "<UNSET>", and a single instance `UNSET = _Unset()`.
It is used as a default parameter value when `None` cannot be used, because the code must distinguish an explicitly passed `None` from a parameter not being provided.
With the singleton, only one `_Unset` instance exists in memory regardless of how many function calls or parameter checks occur; every parameter default holds a reference to the same object.
If `_Unset()` were instantiated repeatedly (e.g. `def foo(arg=_Unset())` or per call), thousands of parameter checks would create thousands of separate objects.
Each separate instance would consume memory for object header/metadata, an instance dictionary (even if empty), and reference overhead.
The singleton is reused across the codebase, e.g. `gridspec.py` `update()` (around line 370) uses `_UNSET` as defaults for left, bottom, right, top, wspace, hspace.

`Artist.set()` dynamically generates signatures with `_api.UNSET` defaults for many properties (artist.py around line 163), so potentially hundreds of parameter definitions share the same singleton instance.

Identity comparisons such as `if left is not _UNSET:` are efficient with a singleton, since identity checks are faster than equality checks and the singleton guarantees the same object identity throughout the codebase.

ConnectionError is a subclass of RequestException (exceptions.py line 59), placing it in the base exception hierarchy of requests.
ConnectionError specifically represents network/transport-level failures that occur before or during connection establishment, such as DNS failure or refused connections.

It is distinguished from other RequestException subclasses that cover different failure categories: HTTPError (4xx/5xx status responses after a successful connection), Timeout, InvalidURL/URLRequired (URL validation problems), and TooManyRedirects (redirect loops).

In adapters.py, ClosedPoolError (lines 679-680) is converted to ConnectionError.
In models.py (line 826), a ReadTimeoutError during reading of response data can be raised as ConnectionError.
More specific connection-related errors inherit from ConnectionError: ProxyError (line 63), SSLError (line 67), and ConnectTimeout (line 80, which also inherits from Timeout).

Converting low-level errors to ConnectionError gives users a consistent interface for network failures, allowing both broad handling (catch ConnectionError) and specific handling (ProxyError, SSLError).

The separation lets users handle error types appropriately, e.g. retrying network connection failures while handling HTTPError based on status code; docs/user/quickstart.rst (lines 553-554) states ConnectionError is raised for network problems, distinct from HTTP-level errors.

The normalization constant Z in the robust soliton distribution class computes a partial sum of reciprocal integers: z = sum(1/i) for i from 1 to round(k/R) - 1, where R = c * log(k/delta) * k^0.5.
The harmonic sum in Z corresponds to the robust component tau, whose terms have the form R/(k*x) for x from 1 to round(k/R) - 1.
Z adds a logarithmic correction term log(R/delta) to the harmonic sum.
The log(R/delta) correction matches the special case of tau at x = round(k/R), whose value is R*log(R/delta)/k.
The combined sum (harmonic sum plus log correction) is multiplied by R/k and added to 1: Z = 1 + z*R/k.
The factor R/k scales the sum to properly normalize the robust component tau, while the +1 accounts for the ideal soliton component rho.
The pmf is (rho + tau)/Z, so dividing by Z makes the probabilities sum to unity over the support {1, 2, ..., k}, because Z equals the total mass of rho + tau.

The VOTable 1.2+ specification mandates that UCD strings conform to the UCD1+ controlled vocabulary standard, which is why stricter validation is enforced.

Conan is a cross-platform C/C++ package manager that must support a wide variety of compilers and target platforms, so the flag generation logic in flags.py has complex branching that needs testing across them.
Different compilers use different flag syntax for the same purpose, e.g. GCC uses -m64 for 64-bit, MSVC uses no architecture flag, and Intel uses /Qm64 on Windows but -m64 on Linux.

Architecture flags depend on the compiler, architecture and OS combination (e.g. x86 gives -m32, s390 gives -m31, armv7 gives no flag, and ppc32/ppc64 on AIX give -maix32/-maix64), so the tests are parametrized over compiler, arch and OS.

Different compiler versions support different C++ standards with different flag names, e.g. GCC 4.6 uses -std=c++0x for C++11, while GCC 4.7 and later use -std=c++11, and C++14 is unsupported before 4.8 and uses -std=c++1y at 4.8 versus -std=c++14 at 4.9.

Build type optimization/debug flags differ completely between compilers (e.g. MSVC Debug gives -Zi -Ob0 -Od, GCC Debug gives -g, sun-cc Release gives -xO3 versus GCC's -O3), so Debug, Release, RelWithDebInfo and MinSizeRel are tested for each compiler.
Special cases such as the vs_toolset (e.g. v140_clang_c2 with msvc), Catalyst subsystem on macOS, AIX PowerPC and clang-cl on Windows change the flags and must be tested.
The tests prevent regressions: changes to flag logic must not break edge cases or backward compatibility with existing configurations.
Incorrect flags can cause compilation failures or binaries that crash, so any mistake in flag generation can break users' builds.

Flag generation is not a simple mapping but depends on the intersection of compiler vendor, compiler version, target architecture, operating system and build configuration, so comprehensive parametrized testing covers the whole matrix.
The `messages` property of `ValidationError` (django/core/exceptions.py, around lines 193-196) returns a flat list of error messages and works for both dictionary-based and list-based error storage.
ValidationError supports two internal storage formats: `error_dict`, a dict mapping field names to lists of ValidationError instances, and `error_list`, a flat list of ValidationError instances.
The `__iter__` method (around lines 206-215) is the unified aggregation/iteration layer for both formats, and `messages` reuses it instead of iterating the stored errors itself.
For `error_dict`, `__iter__` yields `(field, list(ValidationError(errors)))` tuples, normalizing each error list into ValidationError instances.
For `error_list`, `__iter__` yields formatted string messages, applying parameter substitution when `error.params` exists.
For `error_dict`, `messages` returns `sum(dict(self).values(), [])`. `dict(self)` calls `__iter__`, and `sum` flattens the lists of lists into one list.
For `error_list`, `messages` returns `list(self)`, which also calls `__iter__`.
`message_dict` uses `dict(self)` and `messages` uses `dict(self)` or `list(self)`, so both go through the same `__iter__` and share normalization and formatting.

Redundant traversal is avoided because `messages` does not manually iterate `self.error_dict` or `self.error_list` and format each error. The iteration, normalization and formatting logic sits in one place, `__iter__`.

Because `__iter__` is the single source of truth, any change to error formatting or normalization there automatically propagates to both `message_dict` and `messages`, which keeps behavior consistent and avoids code duplication.

The validation is in Blueprint.__init__ in src/flask/sansio/blueprints.py (around lines 198-199): `if "." in name: raise ValueError("'name' may not contain a dot '.' character.")`.

Allowing dots would break endpoint naming and make endpoint resolution for nested blueprints impossible; the constraint reserves dots exclusively as hierarchy delimiters.

The test case overridden_final_method_py38.py validates the checker's detection of methods decorated with typing.final that are overridden in a subclass.
The test uses the @final decorator because it marks a method as not overridable, enforcing method immutability across inheritance hierarchies.
Enforcing final methods maintains behavioral contracts, which are fundamental to the Liskov Substitution Principle (LSP).
LSP requires that subclasses be substitutable for their base classes without breaking functionality.

If a base class marks a method @final, it establishes a contract that the method's behavior is immutable and critical to the class's functionality; overriding would violate it and could break code relying on the base behavior.
The detection is implemented in the _check_invalid_overridden_method method in pylint/checkers/classes/class_checker.py (around lines 1503-1511).
The checker determines the parent method is final by calling decorated_with(parent_function_node, ["typing.final"]) or uninferable_final_decorators(parent_function_node.decorators).
When a subclass overrides a final method, the checker emits the overridden-final-method warning (W0239).
The @final decorator is available since Python 3.8 per PEP 591, hence the py38 in the test name.
In the test file, Subclass overriding Base.my_method(), which is decorated with @final, is flagged as a violation (line 15).
The design still allows polymorphism for non-final methods while keeping critical final methods predictable.

The discovered accesses are used to build a dependency map.

When caching is used, __get__ calls fget to populate the cache when it is stale.
Recomputation trigger: fget is invoked when needs_update detects that dependencies have changed.
Re-invoking fget on dependency changes ensures state consistency.
Together this enables automatic reactive computed properties without the user manually specifying dependencies.
InvalidSchema uses dual inheritance from both RequestException and ValueError, giving two semantic perspectives on the same error condition.
The RequestException perspective categorizes the error as a request/network I/O operation failure, since RequestException inherits from IOError (changed from RuntimeError as of Requests 2.0).
Inheriting RequestException allows the error to be caught as part of the Requests exception hierarchy, enabling generic handling of all request-related errors.
RequestException.__init__() stores request and response attributes, which are available for debugging.
The ValueError perspective categorizes the error as a value validation failure: the URL scheme value itself is invalid or unsupported.
Inheriting ValueError allows the exception to be caught by code that handles general Python value validation errors, not just Requests-specific errors.
InvalidSchema is raised when no connection adapter is found for a URL scheme (sessions.py:792), with message "No connection adapters were found for {url!r}".
InvalidSchema is raised when SOCKS proxy dependencies are missing (adapters.py:63), with message "Missing dependencies for SOCKS support."
The same dual-inheritance pattern (RequestException, ValueError) is used by other validation-related exceptions in the module: MissingSchema, InvalidURL, and InvalidHeader.
The design allows flexible error handling: callers can catch it either as a Requests-specific error or as a general value validation error, depending on their strategy.

For binary classification, the default differs: in _get_response_values (sklearn/utils/_response.py, around lines 211-212), when pos_label is None and target type is binary, pos_label = classes[-1].
In binary classification classes[-1] equals classes[1], so the default is the second class.
For multi-class targets, labels are binarized with label_binarize (around line 265 of _ranking.py), and the fixed pos_label of 1 is used for the subsequent binary metric calculations.
The hard-coded value of 1 ensures consistency when converting multi-class problems into binary sub-problems for metric computation.

The dialect's UnorderedSelectStatementSegment uses copy() and insert() on the parent's grammar to preserve the parent (ANSI) class's grammar structure and allow incremental extension, rather than defining match_grammar from scratch.
Defining match_grammar from scratch would discard/replace the parent's grammar structure, whereas child classes inheriting from parent segment classes need to extend it.
match_grammar is a class variable of BaseSegment (defined in src/sqlfluff/core/parser/segments/base.py around line 163).
The copy() method (in src/sqlfluff/core/parser/grammar/base.py, starting around line 240) creates a shallow copy of the grammar and allows new elements to be inserted via the insert parameter.

Using copy() with insert allows dialect-specific clauses (e.g. IntoClauseSegment, QualifyClauseSegment) to be added at specific positions using the before parameter, without duplicating the entire base grammar.
In dialect_postgres.py (around lines 1781-1796), the PostgreSQL UnorderedSelectStatementSegment copies the ANSI grammar and inserts IntoClauseSegment before FromClauseSegment.

In dialect_ansi.py (around lines 2836-2857), SelectStatementSegment uses UnorderedSelectStatementSegment.match_grammar.copy() to add ORDER BY and other clauses, with a comment saying 'Inherit most of the parse grammar from the unordered version.'

A comment in dialect_postgres.py (around line 1800) says 'Overrides ANSI as the parse grammar copy needs to be reapplied', indicating that simply overriding match_grammar would break the inheritance chain.
The composition pattern keeps all parent grammar elements while child classes add dialect-specific features incrementally.
This pattern is used consistently across multiple dialects (PostgreSQL, Oracle, MySQL, Snowflake, BigQuery, etc.) extending the ANSI base.

The registry allows new validators to be added without altering the core validation logic.

Semantic versioning for the validation library helps maintain compatibility.

Synchronization is achieved by coordinating both the bounds update and the tick recalculation within a single method, `adjust_bounds`, which checks for infinite values before performing either operation.
The implementation is in `sympy/plotting/pygletplot/plot_axes.py`, in the `adjust_bounds` method (around lines 98-107).
`adjust_bounds` loops over the three axes (range(3)) and compares the child bounds against the axes' bounding box.
When a child bound for an axis is infinite (abs(c[i][0]) or abs(c[i][1]) is S.Infinity), the method uses `continue` to skip that axis.
The `continue` skips both the bounding box update and the tick recalculation call together, so the two are never out of step for that axis.

When the values are finite, the bounding box is updated (min of the lower bounds, max of the upper bounds, or the child's value if the box entry is None), then `self._bounding_box` is set and `_recalculate_axis_ticks(i)` is called.
Tick calculation logic is isolated in a separate method, `_recalculate_axis_ticks` (around lines 109-115), while `adjust_bounds` orchestrates both operations.
Child plot objects such as `PlotCurve` and `PlotSurface` initialize their bounds with `S.Infinity` and `S.NegativeInfinity` as placeholders.
Skipping infinite placeholder bounds prevents invalid coordinate ranges from affecting the axes' bounds and tick marks in the visualization.

Stage 1 tests valid grid_mapping formats: a single mapping "crs: x y", multiple mappings "crs: x y crs2: lat lon", and a stray-colon form "crs: x y crs2 : lat lon".
The stray-colon case is handled by the implementation in xarray/conventions.py by replacing " :" with ":".

Stage 2 tests an invalid grid_mapping "crs x y crs2: lat lon" (missing colon after "crs"), which must raise a ValueError matching "misses ':'"; the implementation checks whether the first element lacks a colon.
Stage 3 moves to formula_terms validation: a valid value "A: lat D: lon E: crs2" is parsed, while a malformed "A: lat lon D: crs E: crs2" triggers a UserWarning.
grid_mapping and formula_terms use different parsing logic: grid_mapping extracts the keys from the parsed key-value structure, while formula_terms extracts the values (variable names).
They also have different error handling: grid_mapping raises ValueError for missing colons, whereas formula_terms only warns about malformed content and continues processing.
Testing valid cases first (progressive validation) confirms the parser works correctly before testing error cases.
The approach gives comprehensive coverage of decode_cf_variables behavior for coordinate-related attributes.

The entry point is GraphAPI._load_root_consumer_conanfile() in conan/api/subapi/graph.py (about lines 20-50).
_load_root_consumer_conanfile is called by GraphAPI.load_graph_consumer() for consumer conanfiles and by GraphAPI.load_root_test_conanfile() for test_package conanfiles.

It first creates a ConanApp(self._conan_api), which builds the infrastructure: ConanBasicApp with PkgCache, auth manager, RemoteManager and EditablePackages, plus ConanProxy, RangeResolver, PyRequireLoader and ConanFileLoader.
For .py recipes it calls app.loader.load_consumer(), which calls load_named(), which calls load_basic_module(). For .txt files it calls app.loader.load_conanfile_txt() instead.
load_basic_module() checks the _cached_conanfile_classes cache, then parses the Python file with _parse_conanfile(), which takes _load_python_lock and calls _load_python_file() and _parse_module().

_load_python_file() creates a unique module id, adjusts sys.path, loads the module with importlib spec_from_file_location and exec_module, validates required_conan_version, and cleans up module imports.

load_basic_module() calls PyRequireLoader.load_py_requires() to resolve python_requires. This resolves references (graph lock or RangeResolver), loads each one through ConanProxy.get_recipe(), and recursively calls load_basic_module(). It also handles python_requires_extend by modifying the class bases.
ConanProxy.get_recipe()/_get_recipe() checks editables and the local cache (PkgCache.get_latest_recipe_revision), downloads from remotes via RemoteManager if needed, and updates the recipe LRU.

load_basic_module() also sets recipe_folder and recipe_path, loads conandata.yml with yaml.safe_load via _load_data(), caches the class, instantiates the conanfile, and calls its init() method if defined.
load_named() validates name, version, user and channel and calls set_name() and set_version() if defined. load_consumer() then sets display_name, output scope and _conan_is_consumer = True.

load_conanfile_txt() loads the file contents and calls _parse_conan_txt(). This builds a base ConanFile from the requires, tool_requires, test_requires, layout, generators and options sections, then sets _conan_helpers and _conan_is_consumer.

After loading, initialize_conanfile_profile() (conan/internal/graph/profile_node_definer.py) computes per-package settings for host and build profiles through _per_package_settings() and _initialize_conanfile(). It sets settings, buildenv, runenv, conf, settings_build and settings_target.

Finally a RecipeReference is built from the conanfile name, version, user and channel, and the profile options are scoped to it if it has a name. A root Node is created with recipe=RECIPE_CONSUMER and should_build=True.
run_validators() executes a field's validators and aggregates validation errors; it is found in django/forms/fields.py (around line 186) and django/db/models/fields/__init__.py (around line 782).
The method returns early if the value is in self.empty_values, otherwise it loops over self.validators, calling each in a try/except that catches ValidationError.
On each caught ValidationError it checks hasattr(e, "code") and e.code in self.error_messages, and if so overrides e.message with the field's custom error message for that code.
It collects errors by calling errors.extend(e.error_list) for each failing validator and raises a single ValidationError(errors) if any errors were collected.
The hasattr(e, "code") check adds attribute-lookup overhead on every caught ValidationError, which accumulates under high load with many validators.
The repeated errors.extend(e.error_list) calls add overhead: they access e.error_list and extend the list (possibly reallocating), creating repeated list operations when many validators raise errors.
Refactoring: replace hasattr() with getattr(e, "code", None) or a try/except AttributeError around direct access to e.code, which reduces per-iteration overhead.
Refactoring: collect the error lists first (e.g. append e.error_list to a list) and flatten them once, rather than repeatedly extending a list.
Refactoring: use itertools.chain.from_iterable to flatten the collected error lists more efficiently.
Another suggestion is to cache attribute-check results or use a set of known error types if the same ValidationError types are raised repeatedly.

The most impactful optimization is claimed to be replacing hasattr() with getattr(e, "code", None) and using itertools.chain() for list concatenation, since they reduce per-iteration overhead in the hot path.
`save_session` in `src/flask/sessions.py` calls `get_signing_serializer(app)` every time it serializes session data (via `.dumps(dict(session))`).
Each call to `get_signing_serializer` creates a new `URLSafeTimedSerializer` instance, which carries cryptographic setup overhead.
Each call also rebuilds the key list, checking `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS` and constructing the key chain.
The serializer is configured with constant parameters: salt `cookie-session`, `key_derivation` hmac, the `digest_method`, and the `session_json_serializer`.
Under high concurrency many requests modify sessions at once, each triggering `save_session` and a fresh serializer instantiation, so the overhead accumulates across requests.

The serializer configuration (`app.secret_key`, `SECRET_KEY_FALLBACKS`, salt, key derivation, digest method) does not change between requests for the same app instance, so the repeated instantiation is wasteful.
Root cause: `SecureCookieSessionInterface` does not cache or memoize serializer instances.

Optimization: cache the serializer per application instance (for example in a weak-reference dictionary keyed by app), store it as an instance variable and invalidate it only when the secret keys change, or use lazy initialization with memoization.
Caching would eliminate the repeated cryptographic setup and improve performance under high concurrency.
The blend_mode parameter of LightSource.shade_rgb implements a plugin-like architecture using a dictionary-based lookup with a fallback to invoking the value as a callable.

If blend_mode is a key in the lookup dictionary, the corresponding method is called as lookup[blend_mode](rgb, intensity, **kwargs).
If blend_mode is not in the dictionary, it is treated as a custom callable and invoked as blend_mode(rgb, intensity, **kwargs) inside a try block.
Custom callables must match the signature func(rgb, intensity, **kwargs).
If calling blend_mode raises a TypeError (i.e., it is not callable), the exception is caught and a ValueError is raised, chained from the original TypeError.
The ValueError message states that "blend_mode" must be callable or one of the lookup keys (the valid predefined options).
The implementation is in lib/matplotlib/colors.py, around lines 3726-3738.
The design allows extensibility without modifying the core method, since new blending strategies can be supplied as callables.
The predefined methods (blend_hsv, blend_soft_light, blend_overlay) implement different algorithms for combining RGB arrays with an illumination intensity map to produce shaded relief.
The functools cache decorator (lru_cache) creates a persistent mapping between function arguments and their computed return values.
The mapping is stored in an internal cache dictionary that persists across function calls.
The function arguments (as a tuple) serve as the cache key, and the corresponding return values are the cache values.
Unlike normal calls, where arguments and return values are ephemeral, the cache keeps the mapping in memory so later calls with the same arguments return the cached result without recomputation.
The cache holds references to both the arguments (keys) and the return values (values), creating a persistent link between them that outlives the call's execution.
In the test file method_cache_max_size_none.py, a function taking a parameter and returning its incremented value yields the mapping (param_value,) → param_value + 1.
Each unique input argument value maps to its own incremented result, and this mapping persists across multiple calls.
Pylint's stdlib checker (pylint/checkers/stdlib.py, lines 726-766) checks for this pattern, particularly when maxsize=None.
With maxsize=None the cache is unbounded, so it keeps all argument values (and the self reference for instance methods) alive indefinitely, preventing garbage collection.
The relationship becomes a persistent, stateful mapping that can grow unbounded when maxsize=None, unlike normal function execution where the relationship exists only during the call.

`_find_error_handler` in `src/flask/sansio/app.py` (around lines 823-846) creates performance overhead by linearly traversing the exception class's MRO.
The method uses three nested loops: over HTTP status codes `(code, None)` (or `(None,)` if there is no code), over blueprint names `(*blueprints, None)`, and over `exc_class.__mro__`.
The innermost loop (line 841), `for cls in exc_class.__mro__`, does `handler_map.get(cls)` for each class and returns the first non-None handler. This is the critical bottleneck.
The `__mro__` contains the full chain of parent classes, so for deep exception hierarchies each class must be checked sequentially, ending in Exception, BaseException and object.
Complexity is O(n × m × k): n is the number of codes to check (typically 1-2), m is the number of blueprint names plus the app-level None, and k is the MRO depth (5-10+ for complex hierarchies).
In the worst case, when handlers are registered only for base classes such as `Exception` or `ValueError`, or when none match, the whole MRO is traversed before a match is found.
Each MRO class costs one dictionary lookup, repeated for every code and blueprint combination, which multiplies the overhead.
Example: an MRO of 7 classes, 3 blueprints (4 names with the app) and 2 codes gives up to 2 × 4 × 7 = 56 dictionary lookups.
Early termination when a handler is found is already implemented, but it does not remove the worst-case cost.

Suggested optimizations: cache MRO traversal results per exception class, use a pre-computed handler mapping keyed by exception class, or reverse the lookup order if handlers are usually registered for specific exceptions.
